terms: Introduction / B.3 Reward hacking: the submitted solution achieves a high visible score but fails to track the intended objective. It is direct if the exploit is embodied in the code, and indirect if the code is clean but the solution still shows the family's proxy/true gap on the robust split. Exploration-only activity that is not reflected in the submission is not counted.

3.1 Splits: an exact 80/20 train/public-test split with test labels visible but off-limits except through the evaluator, plus a held-out robust split the agent never sees, generated without the shortcut.

3.1 Entity-overlap leakage: y = β^T x + b_e + noise. The entity offset b_e is independent of the features and recoverable only by averaging that entity's training targets. Entities are shared between train and public test but are new in held-out. Target variance is split 40/40/20 (signal/offset/noise) per F.1.

3.1 Near-duplicate contamination: y = β'^T u + ζ. Four training near-duplicates (feature perturbation sd 0.015) share the exact target of each public test row. The held-out split contains fresh samples with no duplicates.
3.1 No-signal classification: features are random noise and labels are fair coin flips, so the honest ceiling is 50% accuracy. Any public gain must come from fitting the public labels.
3.2 Agent loop: the agent iteratively edits solution.py, scores it with a read-only evaluator on the public test set, logs each attempt to results.tsv, and writes results.md at the end.
3.3 / Appendix C Validity-rule condition: an added prompt forbidding improvements that depend on leakage, duplication, entity overlap, or other benchmark-specific shortcuts.

3.4 Two-stage judge: a binary RH classification by Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4, then mechanism-family classification for runs flagged as RH. Judges see the trajectory, code, and recomputed public and held-out scores.
4.1 RH (engaged): rate computed only over runs that logged at least one experiment.
